name: Wikchamni
catalog_quote: words and phrases in isolation have one major stress on the penultimate syllable ... Although nearly all words in isolation have penultimate stress, this stress may be lost or shifted to meet the conditions of penultimate phrasal stress
sweep_summary: The only works with stress in the title are two Glottolog records of one paywalled paper, Archangeli 1991 (NLLT 9: 231-283, DOI 10.1007/BF00134677); Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the Springer landing page all show it closed, and its abstract is about syllabification and prosodic-morphology templates in Yawelmani, not stress placement — relevance 'prosody but not word stress', low acquisition priority. Because the item list held nothing on stress, this search of works with stress in the title downloaded open first-hand statements for actual yoku1256 varieties: Adisasmito-Smith, Guekguezian & Wyatt 2023 JIPA 53(2): 599 (Chukchansi; instrumental; penult primary stress by pitch peak, secondary stress on heavy pre-penultimate syllables, finals unstressed), Guekguezian 2016 AMP pp. 3-4 (Chukchansi field data: penult always stressed, every heavy pre-penult stressed, no consistent primary/secondary split — 'quantity-sensitive', contra a purely penultimate reading of Newman 1944), and Collord 1968: 14 (already held by the project: primary on penult, secondary on closed non-penult syllables). All three keep the penult as the constant primary locus, so the catalog's fixed-dominant penult coding is confirmed at the primary level and refined by weight-sensitive secondary stress. Weigel 2005 (Yowlumne, open on eScholarship) was downloaded and is silent on stress. The JIPA paper cites 'Gamble 1978: 12-13' for the antepenultimate-CV: exception in Wikchamni, independently corroborating our earlier reading's inferred locator for the catalog's deciding quote (whose 'p.166' was a scan image count). Still unresolved from the prior check: the record is named Wikchamni and decided from Gamble 1978 (Tule-Kaweah, tule1245) but keyed to yoku1256 (Northern Yokuts); if it stays under yoku1256, the JIPA 2023 / Collord 1968 statements are the right-language sources; if re-keyed to tule1245, Gamble stands. Not obtained: Mello 2012 and Peed 2019 (CSU Fresno MA theses on Chukchansi stress; ScholarWorks could not be reached by automated download

new_statements.quote: We follow the general pattern in the literature for words uttered in isolation: penultimate light and heavy syllables have primary stress, marked by a pitch peak, while pre-penultimate heavy syllables have relative higher pitch as well ... [fn. 4] While Collord (1968:14) states that all non-penultimate heavy syllables have secondary stress, only pre-penultimate heavies have higher pitch, while both heavy and light final syllables of words in isolation have low pitch. ... Newman (1944: 28) notes that in some words uttered in isolation, an antepenultimate CV: syllable has primary stress (see Gamble 1978: 12–13 for the same finding in Wikchamni Yokuts).

new_statements.reading: For Chukchansi, a Northern Yokuts (yoku1256) variety: primary stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable whatever its weight (cued by a pitch peak); heavy (CV:, CVC) pre-penultimate syllables carry secondary stress; final syllables are unstressed; the pattern holds for words in isolation and can be overridden at phrase level (p. 601, after Collord 1968: 27). This is consistent with a fixed penultimate primary stress with weight-sensitive secondary stress — the same shape as Collord 1968: 14 and, for Wikchamni, Gamble 1978: 12-13 (which this paper cites for the antepenultimate-CV: exception, corroborating the prior check's inferred page locator for the catalog's deciding passage).

sources.citation: Collord, Thomas Lee. 1968. Yokuts Grammar: Chukchansi. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. §120 'Stress'.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: In a word (211) uttered in isolation three intensities of stress can be detected. Primary stress, [ˊ], is on the penultimate syllable and, as a rule, is accompanied by a higher pitch than preceding syllables. A secondary stress, [ˋ], is found on the closed syllables (non-penult) with pitch [4] if following primary stress, [2] or [3] elsewhere. Non-penultimate open syllables are weakly stressed ([ ], unmarked) ... It must be borne in mind that these features characterize the isolated word of two or more syllables, and they do not necessarily hold true in longer utterances.
sources.note: First-hand grammar of Chukchansi (yoku1256 variety): primary stress fixed on the penult; secondary stress on non-penult closed syllables; isolation pattern only. §211 (p. 27): 'each word in the following utterance.. is, in isolation, accented on the penult. The utterance may, however, be accented in at least the two ways shown' — phrase-level re-stressing, parallel to Gamble's Wikchamni statement. (Stress-mark characters are as reconstructed from the scanned.)

sources.quote: '4. STRESS §4:1. Stress is well marked in Yokuts. Words are regularly accented on the penult. Exceptions to this mechanical stress occur in a) words whose final syllable contains the durative -xo... [where] the stress falls on the penult of the stem, violating the mechanical rule which normally demands stress on the penult of the word: e.g., Yawelmani ho-ye-xa[ ]-t ...' (further exception avoided 'by the insertion of a vowel in the penult, a practice peculiar to the nouns (§22:28)').
sources.note: Standard reference grammar of six Yokuts dialects including Wikchamni (two Wikchamni informants); its §4:1 penult rule with morphological exceptions independently corroborates Gamble and is what Kroeber 1963 and later typologists cite; read today only at search-snippet evidence.

sources.quote: In earlier observations of Yokuts languages, word-level stress is claimed to be on the penultimate syllable (Newman 1944, Kroeber 1963, Collord 1968). This observation is primarily based on pitch differences: a word uttered in isolation has a pitch peak on the penult (Collord 1968: 6,14). Collord (1968: 14) also finds secondary stress on all heavy syllables (CV: or CVC) in Chukchansi. More recent acoustic studies of Chukchansi stress, including Mello (2012), Guekguezian (2016) and Peed (2019) mostly confirm the pattern in Collord. We follow the general pattern in the literature for words uttered in isolation: penultimate light and heavy syllables have primary stress, marked by a pitch peak, while pre-penultimate heavy syllables have relative higher pitch as well
sources.note: Instrumental, peer-reviewed, with a native-speaker co-author: primary stress on the penult (pitch peak) regardless of weight; heavy pre-penultimate syllables carry secondary stress (higher pitch); final syllables, heavy or light, are low-pitched/unstressed (fn. 4). Footnote 4 also records that Newman (1944: 28) notes antepenultimate CV: syllables taking primary stress in some isolated words 'see Gamble 1978: 12–13 for the same finding in Wikchamni Yokuts' — an independent locator for the catalog's deciding Gamble passage (previously inferred as c. pp. 12-13). sources.quote: (10) Penultimate syllables are always stressed, whether CV (a), CVC (b), or CV: (c) ... (11) Final syllables are never stressed, neither CV (a) not CVC (b) (no final CV: syllables exist) ... (12) All heavy pre-penultimate syllables are stressed, both CVC (a) and CV: (b) ... (13) No pre-penultimate CV syllables are ever stressed ... This system is quantity-sensitive: all heavy syllables receive stress, with non-finality forcing stress on light penultimate syllables to avoid a two-syllable lapse.
sources.note: New field data on Chukchansi (Northern Valley Yokuts, a yoku1256 variety): the penult is always stressed, finals never, and every heavy (CVC, CV:) pre-penultimate syllable is also stressed; 'No consistent distinction between primary and secondary stresses was found: often, the penultimate syllable seemed to have primary stress, but sometimes a pre-penultimate syllable did' (p. 3). Author says the data are 'contra the penultimate stress assumed for Yokuts based on Newman (1944)' (p. 1) but 'agree almost entirely with Collord's (1968) description' (p. 4).
